newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says no to five-nation meeting on Russia.
newsitem.headline: Italy says no to five-nation meeting on Russia.

text.p: Italy reaffirmed its opposition on Tuesday to the idea of a meeting between NATO's four major powers and Russia to discuss the alliance's expansion plans.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told parliament that he doubted that the meeting would take place and said NATO issues had to be discussed by all 16 members of the alliance.
"The level of NATO enlargement and Russia's attitude concern all the countries that make up NATO," Dini told a joint meeting of the lower house defence and foreign affairs commissions.

"Therefore, since any decision requires the consent of all member countries, we believe that when you discuss these things you need a meeting of...all member countries and not groups which try to conduct separate negotiations," Dini said.

Moscow is bitterly opposed to NATO plans to expand into former communist eastern Europe, arguing that it would threaten domestic security and could undermine President Boris Yeltsin's already shaky political position.

French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl have backed the idea of holding a meeting in the coming months between Russia, the United States, Britain, France and Germany to allow Moscow a chance to discuss expansion plans.
Such a meeting would precede a scheduled summit of the NATO alliance in July that is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance.

The United States has responded coolly to the mooted five-power meeting. The issue of NATO's expansion is expected to figure high on the agenda of a planned meeting between Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Finland next month.
Dini said the planned Clinton-Yeltsin summit rendered the mooted five-nation meeting less likely.
"It very probably won't take place," he said.

He said Italian opposition was not dictated by Rome's exclusion from any meeting. "The problem would be the same even if we were invited. We are dealing here with issues of principle about how NATO works," Dini said.
